description: We are Team Madar from Egypt, six students from New Cairo Technological University passionate about space, games and learning by doing. Our skills cover game logic, 3D interface with Three.js, and data and storytelling. We are building a 3D space mission design game where every design choice has a visible consequence. We would love teammates who bring 3D art or animation, UI/UX design, sound design, or NASA data analysis. Join us and learn mission design by failing safely.
summary:
MissionForge is a browser-based 3D game where players become a mission team and design a real robotic space mission from start to finish. You walk through a mission facility, choose instruments, power, communications, propulsion and a launch vehicle, carry the parts by hand, install them on the spacecraft, fuel it, pass a Go/No-Go review and launch. The flight then plays out with real orbit physics and random emergencies based on problems NASA actually faced. The debrief traces success or failure back to the player's own decisions and compares the design with the real mission.

Four missions unlock in order: a Lunar Orbiter (inspired by LRO), a Mars Orbiter (MRO), a Mars Lander (InSight) and a Europa Flyby Explorer (Europa Clipper), using real instrument mass, power and cost figures from NASA and JPL sources. One to four players share four engineering roles, on one screen or online.

MissionForge answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning the real trade-offs of mission design (mass, power, data, budget and risk) into hands-on decisions, so students learn why every component choice matters. It runs in any browser, with no installation or login.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MissionForge puts the player inside a 3D mission facility: a central Assembly Hall with the spacecraft and ten themed rooms around it (four instrument labs, power, communications, protection and entry, propulsion and fueling, the launch vehicle hall, and mission control). The player builds a spacecraft step by step, by carrying parts, installing them, pumping propellant and running four pre-launch checks, while watching mass, power, data, propellant and budget against real NASA safety margins.

HOW IT WORKS

- Four missions: Lunar Orbiter (LRO), Mars Orbiter (MRO), Mars Lander (InSight) and Europa Flyby Explorer (Europa Clipper). Three modes: Campaign, Sandbox, and Replay a Real Mission (start from the real NASA design).

- Four roles (Systems Engineer, Science Lead, Launch and Orbit Lead, Budget and Risk Manager). Every stage needs all four to approve before it locks, like a real concurrent engineering team. Solo players get an advisor. Online multiplayer for 1 to 4 players uses a 4-letter room code.

- A Go/No-Go review board in Mission Control: each reviewer gives GO or NO-GO with a reason.

- An educational 3D flight: liftoff, staging, cruise, gravity assists, the asteroid belt, orbit insertion or landing, then the data sent home by radio. The flight panel works through real equations with the player's own design: the rocket equation, Hohmann transfer, Kepler's third law and vis-viva, using NASA planetary constants.

- Random flight emergencies based on real cases (safe mode, comet Siding Spring's dust, collision warnings, the asteroid belt, Juno's propellant valve). The correct answer is what NASA actually did.

- A debrief with the score explained, a cause trace from failure back to the exact decisions that caused it, and a comparison with the real mission.

- Change requests that cost more the later they are made, as in real projects.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students and the public learn systems engineering by doing: why mass drives propellant, why power falls with distance from the Sun, why margins and reviews exist, and why late changes are expensive. Every number shown as real comes from a cited NASA or JPL source, and game assumptions are clearly labelled "approximate". It runs on laptops, tablets and phones with no installation, so classrooms can use it directly.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

JavaScript, React 18, Three.js, Vite, Vitest (tests for the simulation engine), MQTT.js for online multiplayer, the Web Audio API for sound, and GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions for deployment. The simulation engine is plain JavaScript, separate from the 3D layer, and new missions or instruments are added as JSON data with no new code.

CREATIVITY

Instead of menus and sliders, players physically build the spacecraft in 3D, and the game explains which of their own decisions made the mission succeed or fail. Real NASA history becomes playable emergencies, and real missions become a benchmark to beat.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy and source citation, accessibility (touch controls, a low-graphics mode, an interactive tour, optional hints, a glossary), teamwork, and NASA brand rules: no NASA logos are used and no endorsement is implied. All 3D models, textures and sounds are generated in code, so no third-party assets are used.
